blocks.text: December 5th, 1945. 2:10 in the afternoon. Five Navy bombers take off from Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Fourteen men. A routine training flight.
An hour and a half later, the leader's voice comes over the radio. Both my compasses are out.
He is no longer sure which way Florida is. He turns the flight one way. Then another. The sun goes down. The weather turns.
At 7:04 p.m., one pilot calls out to his leader. There is no answer. Then, silence.
The Navy sends a rescue plane. A flying boat with thirteen men on board. It takes off at 7:27. Three minutes later, it makes one radio call. It is never heard from again.
Twenty minutes after that, a passing ship reports a burst of flame on the horizon.
Six aircraft. Twenty-seven men. Gone in a single evening.
For five days, hundreds of planes and ships sweep the ocean. They find nothing. The Navy's final report gives the cause in two words: cause unknown.
Most experts believe the planes simply ran out of fuel over a stormy sea. But nineteen years later, a writer gave that stretch of ocean a name. The Bermuda Triangle.
